newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Taylor leads Liberian poll, rival protests.
newsitem.headline: Taylor leads Liberian poll, rival protests.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor enjoyed a comfortable early lead in Liberia's elections on Monday, taking a first step towards a victory through the ballot box that he failed to achieve by the gun.
Monday newspapers in the capital Monrovia headlined the lead of the man who plunged the West African nation into a seven-year civil war when he invaded from Ivory Coast in 1989.

But as Taylor's fanatical supporters cheered preliminary results giving him a 62 percent lead, his closest rival Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, polling well below expectations with 18 percent, raised charges of poll malpractice.

"In many places outside Montserrado County reports say that (party) observers were excluded from the counting of the votes on the basis that their accreditation cards did not match their names," she told state radio on Monday.
"The only party allowed to stay for the count was the NPP (National Patriotic Party) which is Charles Taylor's party."
Taylor needs 50 percent plus to avoid an August 2 run-off.
Johnson-Sirleaf's allegations of fraud, first aired on radio by her campaign manager Dusty Wolokolie on Sunday, were the first sour note in elections praised by monitors.
Wolokolie accused officials of the Independent Elections Commission (IENEC) and troops of the West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG of interfering with voting at some stations.
"We've heard of widespread fraud on the part of IENEC officials as well as ECOMOG personnel... We have film to show evidence of ECOMOG casting ballots for people," Wolokolie said.

Johnson-Sirleaf said unauthorised people helped some voters. "People did not know how to vote in many areas and needed assistance. During that assistance their intent and wishes were not respected," she added.
Wolokolie was interviewed live on radio from inside the commission headquarters just before elections chief Henry Andrews broadcast the first preliminary results.
ECOMOG soldiers, reacting to the interview, halted the broadcast, forcing Andrews to suspend his statement briefly.

General Victor Malu, commander of the Nigerian-led force, confirmed the action of the soldiers but said they had acted beyond their orders. "They were only told to bring the man (Wolokolie) to substantiate his allegations," Malu told Reuters.

The preliminary official results for about 10 percent of total ballots showed Taylor polling 49,539 votes of 79,403 counted. Johnson-Sirleaf only managed 14,379 votes. No other candidate polled more than six percent.
Taylor supporters, chanting "Taylor has won" poured into the streets of the capital Monrovia, darkened by a long-term nationwide electricity blackout, after hearing the news.
International election experts helping with organisation estimated voter turnout on Saturday at around 85 percent.
A total of just over 700,000 people registered to vote.
Taylor is seen by many as the forceful leader needed in the post-war period. He had superior resources to his rivals. With a national radio station, he ran a well-oiled campaign machine.
Johnson-Sirleaf entered the race late but built up support through her image of integrity and good contacts with donors.
Two other former warlords, Alhaji Kromah and George Boley, also ran. Kromah was in third place with 5.09 percent.
International monitors and Liberia's West African neighbours, who finally rallied the warlords around a peace deal, praised the smooth conduct of the poll.
